core: Pronunciation as the skill of producing and perceiving English sounds
Mutual intelligibility as the goal; all accents are valid; no accent-elimination framing
The sounds of English: vowels and consonants
Word stress: stressed syllables; stress can change meaning (record/record)
Sentence stress and rhythm: content words stressed, function words weak
Intonation: rising for yes/no questions, falling for statements (general patterns)
Connected speech basics: linking and reduction, named simply
Practical practice strategies: listen and imitate, minimal pairs, recording yourself
supporting: Weak forms of grammar words and the schwa vowel in unstressed syllables
How dictionaries mark pronunciation and stress (IPA named, not taught in depth)
UK and US pronunciation variants as legitimate differences
Listen-and-repeat practice modeled by BBC Learning English materials
outOfScope: Conversation skills and turn-taking (sibling topic: conversation-skills)
The International Phonetic Alphabet in depth (named only, as sourced)
Individualized accent coaching or accent-elimination advice

claims.claim: Pronunciation is the skill of producing and perceiving the sounds of a language; its working goal is mutual intelligibility — being understood and understanding others — not the elimination of a learner's accent.
English sounds are organized into two broad classes, vowels and consonants, and learning materials and dictionaries present them that way.

Some English sounds are not found in every language, and some sounds occur in only some varieties of English (for example, UK-only or US-only sounds); this is ordinary language difference, not a deficiency in any speaker.
English words are built from syllables, and most words have one syllable pronounced with more force than the others; dictionaries mark this stress in their pronunciations.

Word stress can distinguish meaning between words with identical spelling: record as a noun is pronounced with stress on the first syllable (/ˈrek.ɔːd/), while record as a verb is pronounced with stress on the second (/rɪˈkɔːd/).

In English sentences, the words that carry the main information (content words such as nouns and main verbs) are typically stressed, while grammar words (function words such as articles and auxiliary verbs) are often weak or reduced.

Intonation — the rise and fall of the voice's pitch — follows general patterns: yes/no questions typically rise at the end, statements typically fall; these are useful starting points rather than rigid rules.

In natural connected speech, words are not separated the way they are in writing: sounds link across word boundaries and some sounds are reduced or dropped; these features are called connected speech.

Practical pronunciation practice includes listening to models and imitating them, comparing minimal pairs (words differing by one sound), and listening back to one's own speech; the BBC materials model this as watch, listen, and repeat.

conflictingEvidence.issue: What counts as the right pronunciation model?
positions: Some materials present a single standard accent as the target for learners.

The professional literature treats model choice as a decision about goals and priorities, and emphasizes intelligibility; a teacher or learner whose accent is not a broadcast standard is not at a disadvantage.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson frames pronunciation around mutual intelligibility and treats all accents as valid, avoiding accent-elimination framing entirely, consistent with the subject's editorial cautions.

sourceRecords.title: BBC Learning English — Pronunciation
sourceRecords.notes: Tier A. Read live on 2026-08-21 (HTTP 200). The section presents Tim's Pronunciation Workshop ("shows you how English is really spoken. It'll help you become a better listener and a more fluent speaker") and The Sounds of English, "our video guide to all the consonant and vowel sounds in the English language. Watch, listen and repeat." Supports: pronunciation as producing and perceiving speech; vowels and consonants; listen-and-repeat practice. Reference only; prose synthesized.

sourceRecords.title: Tim's Pronunciation Workshop: Can
sourceRecords.notes: Tier A. Read live on 2026-08-21 (HTTP 200). States that in fluent everyday English, when the modal auxiliary 'can' is unstressed its pronunciation changes to /kən/, and "This is what's known as a weak form"; the episode closes with a listen-and-repeat segment. Supports: weak forms of function words; sentence stress; listen-and-imitate practice. Reference only.

sourceRecords.title: Tim's Pronunciation Workshop: The
sourceRecords.notes: Tier A. Read live on 2026-08-21 (HTTP 200). Demonstrates that the unstressed definite article 'the' is pronounced /ðə/ before consonant sounds and /ðɪː/ before vowel sounds, with a small linking /j/ possible between vowels. Supports: reduced pronunciations of grammar words and linking in connected speech. Reference only.

sourceRecords.title: Tim's Pronunciation Workshop: Summary
sourceRecords.notes: Tier A. Read live on 2026-08-21 (HTTP 200). Reviews connected speech: speakers "mostly bump the words together"; consonant sounds link with vowel sounds; "Unstressed grammar words are often weak" (e.g. 'I'd have been late' -> /aɪdəv bɪn leɪt/); schwa is "important to the rhythm of natural spoken English"; "These are all features of what we call connected speech." Also advises that the more you listen to and speak English, the more naturally these features come. Reference only.

sourceRecords.title: Cambridge Dictionary — Pronunciation symbols
sourceRecords.notes: Tier A. Read live on 2026-08-21 (HTTP 200). Explains that the dictionary uses the International Phonetic Alphabet (IPA) to show pronunciation in writing, with sections for vowels, consonants, and other sounds; shows primary stress (ˈ, strongest) and secondary stress (ˌ, less strong) and syllable division; notes that some sounds are found only in UK English or only in US English; includes a linking /r/ example ('four apples' /ˌfɔːr ˈæp.əlz/). Supports: IPA named as dictionary notation (not taught in depth); vowel/consonant organization; word stress and syllable division; linking; legitimate UK/US sound differences. Reference only.

sourceRecords.title: Cambridge Dictionary — record
sourceRecords.notes: Tier A. Read live on 2026-08-21 (HTTP 200). The entry shows record as a noun pronounced /ˈrek.ɔːd/ (UK) and as a verb pronounced /rɪˈkɔːd/ (UK) — the same spelling with stress on different syllables. Supports the lesson's word-stress-changes-meaning example. Reference only; the lesson uses its own example sentences.

sourceRecords.title: Language Foundations Handbook — Spelling: Schwa Vowels
sourceRecords.notes: Tier A per the subject's source map. Read live on 2026-08-21 (HTTP 200). Defines the schwa as a vowel that is unstressed, toneless, and neutral, occurring in unstressed syllables (e.g. 'a' in about), and states that schwa vowels are the most common vowel sounds in the English language and sound like "uh"; also lists as prior knowledge the difference between vowels and consonants and the idea that syllables can be stressed or unstressed. Supports: vowel/consonant distinction; stressed vs unstressed syllables; reduced vowels in unstressed syllables. Reference only.

sourceRecords.title: Intonation (article by the TeachingEnglish Editorial Team)
sourceRecords.notes: Tier B. The live site blocks automated access; read the Internet Archive capture of 2013-11-19 (web.archive.org/web/20131119121228/https://www.teachingenglish.org.uk/article/intonation). States intonation is how we say things rather than what we say; gives the general patterns "Wh-word questions: falling intonation; Yes/No questions: rising; Statements: falling" and calls them "starting-points, rather than rules"; notes the tonic syllable is usually a high-content word; advises that learners need greater awareness of intonation to facilitate speaking and listening rather than native-speaker-level pronunciation; suggests providing models, drilling, and imitation. Supports: intonation patterns; content words carrying sentence stress; intelligibility framing; practice strategies. Reference only.

sourceRecords.title: Intonation (Teaching knowledge database)
sourceRecords.notes: Tier B. Read the Internet Archive capture of 2021-09-19 (web.archive.org/web/20210919074443/https://www.teachingenglish.org.uk/article/intonation-0) because the live site blocks automated access. Defines intonation as the way the pitch of a speaker's voice goes up or down as they speak; intonation can be rising, falling, or flat; intonation commonly drops at the end of a sentence to show the speaker has finished. Supports: the general falling pattern at the end of statements. Reference only.

sourceRecords.title: Pronunciation Matters — re-thinking goals, priorities and models (Robin Walker)
sourceRecords.notes: Tier B. Read the Internet Archive capture of 2019-10-16 (web.archive.org/web/20191016175157/https://www.teachingenglish.org.uk/article/pronunciation-matters-re-thinking-goals-priorities-models) because the live site blocks automated access. Robin Walker's talk summary poses the questions of how to choose a model and priorities for pronunciation and "What do we do if our own accent isn't 'BBC'?", treating accent-model choice as a decision rather than a fixed standard. Supports the lesson's framing that pronunciation goals are about intelligibility and priorities, with all accents valid. Reference only.
